newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Barak sees himself as Rabin's heir.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Barak sees himself as Rabin's heir.

text.p: Former army chief Ehud Barak, favoured to win elections on Tuesday for leader of Israel's main opposition Labour party, pledged on Monday to follow the peace legacy of assassinated Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.
"I see myself as his follower and the one to continue his legacy," Barak told a news conference for foreign journalists.

He said the Labour party, which lost national elections a year ago to Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing Likud bloc, was "committed to take calculated risks in the Middle east in order to achieve peace".
Outlining his policy, Barak, 55, said Palestinians must have self-determination, which could lead to a state.

"If they will determine themselves beyond the borders of Israel as they will be shaped in the permanent status negotiations, we will see there...a Palestinian state, maybe with certain limitations on some attributes of sovereignty as a result of our security concerns," Barak said in English.
Security is a keyword for Barak, whose credentials as a top military man could help him tap into Netanyahu's power base of right-wing and religious Israelis.
Prime Minister Netanyahu has proposed giving Palestinians permanent autonomy, citing as a model Puerto Rico, a self-governing territory under the protection of the United States.

"Israel cannot afford and shouldn't try to govern over another people. I think that we should separate ourselves from the Palestinians," Barak said, rejecting the Puerto Rico proposal as a "cheap gimmick".
"We do not need here neither a kind of apartheid nor a Bosnia, and under Netanyahu we might reach both," he said.
But Barak's position paper, distributed at the news conference, on a permanent peace settlement flashed numerous red flags for the PLO.

"No return to the 1967 (pre-Middle East war) borders, united Jerusalem is to remain under Israeli sovereignty, a majority of settlers in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank) to remain under Israeli sovereignty, no foreign army is to be deployed west of the Jordan River," it said.

Barak, foreign minister from 1995 to 1996 in the last Labour government, sidestepped a question on whether he would stop the building of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem which has plunged Middle East peacemaking into crisis.

"I would not initiate (construction) in this timing and I would do the whole thing in a total different sequence of events," he said about project at the site Israel calls Har Homa and Palestinians refer to as Jabal Abu Ghneim.

"I would begin from a sewage project for the Palestinians in East Jerusalem and then continue with a major housing project for (them)...and I would do it in front of the world media and only then would I consider the right timing for Har Homa."
Opinion polls predicted Barak would easily defeat three other candidates to follow former Prime Minister Shimon Peres as Labour leader.

Last month, Barak torpedoed an attempt by Peres supporters to appoint the veteran politician as Labour party president, an honorary position which the ex-general feared could force him into a measure of power-sharing.

It is his experience at running the army and participation in numerous undercover operations during his military career which Barak hopes will establish him as a counterforce to Netanyahu, also a former commando.

"Netanyahu seems to operate out of deep anxiety. He still mentions sometimes Munich and Auschwitz -- kind of deep primal anxieties," Barak said, referring to the effect of the Nazi Holocaust on the right-wing leader's thinking.
"It's a pity. I don't think that Netanyahu is a bad man. He's in a way inexperienced and the wrong man for this job at this time."
